states.summary: The route outlived her. The grain exchange keeps her ledgers in a drawer nobody opens.
She keeps the shelter's stores now, and prices everything twice — once in goods, once in what it cost to get here.

The exchange gave her the southern routes and a stamp. Caravan space is easier to get now, and the rates carry a note: 'friend of the coordinator.' She never mentions the water station. She also never charges you the note.
She rebuilt the route on her own wheels. Trading with her stays fair in a way that is not written down anywhere — she remembers who handed over the antibiotics when nothing was owed.
She organized the factors who now agree, quietly, that your shelter pays surcharge. Nothing is posted. Nothing needs to be. The ledgers all say the same thing because she wrote most of them.

Her second wagon went through the cut road crust. She is camped on the wreck, guarding the cargo with a rifle she does not quite have the strength to use. She names a fair price for help and does not pretend it is charity.
The wreck took her wagon and the drought took her margin. She remembers who bought her shortage at a premium. She will still trade. She will not call it anything but what it is.
Her route goes on the way it always has, one wagon lighter than the ledgers say it should be. She trades on schedule and owes nobody, including you.
A two-wagon caravan factor short on medicine and axle parts after a bad crossing. She trades straight, prices fast, and mentions exactly once that she pays favors back with interest.
The almshouse flies a sheet where her clinic sign was. The camp reads the names she left anyway, in her hand, because nobody can improve on it.
She re-built her clinic inside the shelter with the same two rules: stated odds, and the work gets done anyway. Your infirmary keeps patients she would have had to turn away.

The clinic held. It trains more hands than it loses now, and the verge sends its sick to a door that has never once been shut at the appointed hour. Your people are treated at stated odds and the odds have improved.

Extracted before the outbreak took the building, she now runs a rotating waystation clinic with the coalition. Your expeditions are met by trained hands at two stops, and she bills the ledger, not the shelter.

The clinic outlived her supplies and then her patience. She still answers the door, but the training stopped, and the camp's sick list is a season longer than it was. The almshouse keeps her name off the roster of the lost, at her own instruction.

Your supplies bought the clinic a season. The beds are full of a fever she can name but not stop, and she has started training the recovering to carry what she cannot. She will not ask you to come. She has written to you anyway.
The fever found the almshouse. She works sixteen-hour shifts at stated odds and does not say the word triage where the waiting can hear it.
Eight beds, dwindling shelves, and a standard she refuses to lower. She shows you the inventory before she asks for anything, which is how you know what she is not asking for.
His filed objections outlived him. Somebody keeps them. Nobody has told you who.
He drills your watch the garrison way: posted orders, logged refusals, no exceptions and no favors. The garrison considers him their problem. Your nights disagree.

Escaped with your help, he sends the shelter word before every sweep: routes, timing, the mood of the command. The margins of his messages still carry dated objections, now about the men who hunted him.

The garrison paid what it promised and posted the case where procedure requires. Your shelter's passes are honored a season early and a shade too quickly. The queue has noticed which door you came through.
He kept his post and his objections, and the objections have stopped being dated. The checkpoint honors your papers and nothing else about you.

The margin notes finally exceeded the order. He is sheltering where the sweeps do not look first, and he sent you his field kit for safekeeping — which is deserter for please, and thank you, and I am sorry.
The checkpoint changed hands twice in a season and he is still there, which in the garrison is a kind of survival. Passage is honored to the letter.
A garrison corporal who runs his checkpoint by the book and keeps the book where petitioners can see it. Passage is a transaction. The book is a promise.
Her counting book is kept with the shelter records, in her hand, finished to the last page. Nobody has been able to make themselves close the cover.

She can dress a wound, read a dose aloud, and catch an error before it lands — the last one better than the first two. She teaches the younger ones the counting the way it was taught to her: once, properly, and checked.
She keeps count of the shelter stores, the queue, and the days since anybody was lost. She hums less often than she did at the baths, and checks her work twice before showing anyone.
She sits the lessons the shelter will give and invents the ones it will not. She has begun correcting the arithmetic of people twice her age, who for some reason keep asking her to.
Still at the baths, still counting, kept alive in the way of the queue: everyone's supplies and no one's child. She has stopped asking shelter columns whether they are full.
A child keeping order in a queue that has forgotten why. She is not lost, exactly. Nobody has made her count of the situation wrong yet.
The substation grounds are on, tagged with her badge number and the date. The rebuilders check them on a schedule she wrote and did not sign.
Your generator has never run so boringly. She has opinions about your load schedule and a certification that expired in a world that ended, and both are correct.

The rebuilders gave her the region and she gave it lines that stay up. Two waystation feeders run again on switching orders done safely. Caravans plan around her schedule now, which is the only kind of monument she would accept.
Another faction's colors are on the substation fence and the switching orders are being done unsafely. The lights out here come and go on a schedule nobody publishes.
With your parts she has the main bus dressed and one feeder proving itself daily. The rebuilders have noticed, which means paperwork, which she considers the price of copper.
She is still out there, keeping the compound secure and the grounds checked, running a grid that has no customers yet.
A grid engineer stranded at a live substation with working grounds and no copper. She offers you switching orders and a load calculation before she asks for a single part.
The camps buried her by her own book: the meal, the naming, the silence after. Three camps kept the hour at once, which had not happened before and has not since.

When the camps quarrel now, they send for her before they send for anyone with a rifle. She has turned defending a camp into the argued position that camps are worth defending, and both sides quote her without knowing it.

The evacuation became a teaching and the teaching became a rota: sweep, share, name the dead. Shrines keep her hours in four regions. She finds the word movement embarrassing and the word chore accurate.
She keeps her own hours now, one bowl, one name a day. The camp she would not spend you on still stands, and she has stopped saying so out loud.

The camp she organized holds because she rationed the panic first and the grain second. Raiders test the fence; the pot stays on. She has begun teaching others the rota in case the fence fails on a day she is busy.
The camp keeps its hours: meal, naming, silence. There is soup if you work and a verdict-free evening if you do not.
An elder who runs a refugee camp like a work rota with prayers attached. The rota is the sermon. The sermon is mostly sweeping.
The guild posted her cellars as sealed, which among scavengers is a headstone. The floors she called real have taken two more people who did not believe the posting.
Your salvage returns doubled and your rope budget tripled. She has mapped your shelter's crawlspaces against a fire, a flood, and a siege, and Sleeps badly until all three are answered.
The guild gave her the cellar registry and she gave the guild schedules. Your expeditions get first refusal on finds and floors that are real. The debt is entered, managed, and never once mentioned.
She bought her silence back with your name on it. The guild works the sites ahead of you now, politely, completely, and always by the book — her book.

A cellar floor that was a rumor took her ankle. She is camp-bound, loud about it, and has started dictating her registry to whoever sits still long enough, in case the ankle is the cheap thing she lost.
She works the drowned streets alone, which is the whole plan and most of the risk. Rope for finds, silence extra.
A scavenger who knows which cellar floors are real and is willing to say so for a price. She is faster than you and knows it, and offers to split a find rather than race you for it, once.
The mast still stands. The log ends mid-entry, on schedule, in her neat hand, and somebody out there keeps trying to raise the station that answered on time.

The shelter has a scheduled listening watch now, a logged band calendar, and messages that go out properly. She is teaching two of yours the discipline, which she says is the whole machine; the mast is just wire.

Moved before the seizure reached her, she keys from a new site under a flag that leaves her alone. Your shelter gets the weather copies and, unasked and unlogged, the patrol schedules of people who are not your friends.
She kept the mast and the discipline and added a band of her own: the naming of the moved-on camps, read properly, at a fixed hour. People plan around her schedule now. She logs every one of them.
The garrison got the mast and its operator, and your shelter got the bounty. The station answers on time again. The hand on the key is neater than it used to be, and the log has a second reader.
The faction that maps towers has mapped hers. She keeps transmitting — on schedule, logged — and has started ending each shift by copying the log in two hands, one to send, one to lose.
The mast lives on scavenged cells and inherited discipline. The station answers on schedule and logs everything, including you.
A relay operator keeping a dead network's discipline on live cells. She offers scheduled slots and copies of her signal logs, and asks only that whoever keys back identify honestly.
Half a wagon and a whole debt, both priced daily. He will show you the contract and the buyout figure in the same breath, and the difference between them is his life's work.
Your advance moved the figure within reach. He works the caravan lanes like a man counting steps out of a hole, and quotes your rate first when he quotes anyone.
The Underwrite stamped the buyout and he framed the stamp. His wagons run the crossing roads on schedules he owns outright, and your cargo moves at the founding-member rate forever.
You pressed the debt and bought his routes cheap. He carries what the credit office needs carried now, and his copies of every contract are kept somewhere you will never be shown.
The debt walks with him at its own pace. He negotiates first and everything else second, and neither habit has killed him yet.

The dentist's row chairs are pulled out for cots, and the garrison audit asks different questions than the patients do. He treats first and reconciles later, in the wrong order and the only order that works.

The audit is coming and the third ledger is still unexplained. Your word has started to matter in rooms he cannot enter, and he has started writing down what he owes you, which for him is a form of hope.
Vouched, audited, and still rounding for the living. The overflow clinic trains medics for three neighborhoods now, and the garrison has learned which of its forms he answers fast.
Your testimony made the discrepancy official. The charges fit the entries and miss the mornings, and the overflow queue now waits outside a clinic with nobody willing to sign for the stock.
He treats first and reconciles later, and the reconciling is beginning to keep him up at night.
The plant restart is real and so is the checklist, and the checklist does not care what happened to the night shift. He offers schedules instead of apologies, and the schedules are good.
Your crews passed his checklists, which is more than the last three batches of volunteers managed. He has begun saying the word audit without flinching, which from him is a season changing.

The batching plant runs to a schedule that holds because the crews were trained and the concrete was tested. Your shelter draws from his supply lines at works-manager rates. The gantt chart has your name inked, not penciled.
He restarted the line with skeleton crews and stamped assessments that were technically true. The plant makes the strongest concrete in the region, for a workforce that eats alone.
The schedule is honest. Ask him about the staffing another time.
He sells route copies with the ink still drying and corrects his own map in front of you, which is either honesty or theater and is probably both.

The roll he sold you is already better than the one he sells strangers. He has started walking the toll roads with your corrections folded into his copy, and asking, at intervals, whether your people walked anything he should know about.
His map of the toll country is the map, and your shelter holds one of eleven annotated copies. The eastern road entry has never once needed a correction, and he has never once said why.
He went out to re-walk the one route he never explained and has not come back by any of his own schedules. The map copies keep circulating. His copy has not surfaced.
He sells what he has walked and corrects the roll in public. The eastern road entry is the best thing in it and the only thing he will not discuss.
The crossing log is kept in full view and countersigned by nobody, which is the problem she will describe to you in complete sentences while the queue watches its turn accumulate.
Your mark is in the log now, on the page where the incident reports and the acknowledged reports diverge. She has stopped walking the corridor alone, which is not the same as safe.

The log became the standard: two signatures, full view, no acknowledged-only incidents. Command tolerates her because the bridge works. Your column crosses at the hour her watch owns, and the log says so.
You kept clear of the argument and she kept the log anyway, alone. The corridor is orderly and the crossings are honest and the reports still come back in two versions. She initials both.
The crossing log is kept in full view, countersigned by nobody. Yet.
The annex roof is sound for another season, the lots are tested, and the private tin is not for discussion. She will show you germination rates before she shows you the door.
Your timber is over the annex and the lots are re-sacked. She has started cutting from the private tin for your column's planters, at the same unchanging rate, which is how she says things.

The freehold failed; the annex did not. Half the region's viable planting now traces to lots she held through the bad season, and your shelter's fields are sown from her tested stock under her unamended schedule.
She waited for a better season to move the lots and the roof disagreed with the timetable. The seed library is a wet inventory and a woman who will show you the germination tests anyway, as a lesson.
Tested lots, sound schedule, roof good for another season. The private tin is not for discussion.

The herd ledger and the herd disagree by exactly the animals a hard winter eats, and the well has been dosed since before anyone asked. He is not a liar. Ask him anything except the word that starts with c.

You did the cull arithmetic with him at dawn, out loud, both counting. The milk is thinner and the herd is honest now, and he has started saying the word himself, quietly, to the animals, like an apology.

The allotment's herd is small and true, and its stock is the only breeding line three settlements will take unwitnessed. He doses the well on schedule and teaches cull arithmetic at dawn to anyone who asks.
The sickness found the herd and the ledger found the gap, in that order, in public. He still works the silo. He no longer drinks last, which among allotment people is a verdict.
The herd is fine. The well is dosed. Ask him what you actually need and let us see what the fine herd can afford.
Four notebooks of repeats and a standing offer: he will refute every published solution in writing, including his own, before he lets you fund a fifth notebook.
You fund the notebooks with the warning attached, which no patron before you ever accepted. The repeats have a structure he will not name yet, in case naming it un-named it.

The structure held. The repeat interval resolves to a station keeping time for someone, and the analysis in your shelter's name is the first publication he has signed without a disclaimer in the margins.
You asked for the patron money back and he returned it to the hour, with interest he could not afford. The notebooks are boxed. The understory transmitter answers nobody now.
Four notebooks and a refutation of everything, in writing, available to anyone who brings pencil-paper and does not ask about the early solution.
The pot is honest and the manifest is not, and she is the difference. The queue eats in order of need and the portion ledger disagrees with the pot by exactly the amount the children eat.
Your oil is in her kitchen and your name is in no ledger. The queue has noticed that the bowls got heavier without anyone announcing it, which is how she prefers all improvements to arrive.

The field kitchen feeds the overflow on schedule and in order of need, and the settlement's sick lists got shorter two winters running. Your people eat at her fire when the roads are bad, and nobody audits the portions.
The audit found the arithmetic and never asked what it bought. The queue still arranges itself by need, out of habit, in front of a kitchen that serves the manifest exactly, and thinner.
The pot is honest and the manifest is not. She is the difference, and she will stand in front of that sentence for as long as it takes.
The store mess runs institutional-exact and the food is fair, and there is a crate somewhere in this building that is the only dishonesty in his life and he weighs it daily.

Your amnesty made the crate speakable. He poured the good oil into the mess kettle with the whole rota watching, and cooked differently ever since, in a way nobody can audit because there is nothing left to hide.
He runs provisions for three settlement kitchens now, on institution rules with the lies removed. Your shelter's stores get his count, which is exact, and his advice, which is worth the count.

The crate was real and the exposure was cheaper than the conversation. The mess runs to his old standard under a cook who does not know why the deliveries were always exactly late. He trades oil on the road now, by the flask.
Institutional portions, fair hands, one crate. Ask him which kind of cook he is being today and he will answer honestly and not shortly.
The odds on any road are posted where the driver can read them, and the corner-bearing in his toolbox has a story with two endings. He tells the honest one if you bring grease and patience.

Parts upfront and a witness for the next borrowing: your advance bought the wagon a season and bought him something harder, which is doing it clean. The posted odds on your routes have improved twice.

The Long Walk gave him the fleet and he gave the fleet posted odds and boring axles. Your shelter's wagons are maintained to his standard at caravan rates, and the story with two endings now has the ending where he paid it back in public.

The favor he was owed arrived shaped like a errand he could not refuse, and the wagon runs for other people's freight this season. He still posts the odds. The odds on your routes have quietly widened.
One good wagon kept alive past decency, odds posted where the driver can read them.
The generator runs to stated hours and the private log runs to stated truth, and the intake shed door stays shut when she works alone, which is always.
The brush set you brought is in the generator and the intervals are kept like vows. She has started leaving the private log out on the desk, which for her is a door being left open.
The cut's pump stations hold power on a schedule she publishes and keeps. Your shelter buys off-peak load at rates set in her unrounded hand, and the private log now has a second reader she chose.
You asked about the shed. She answered once, completely, and then drew a line under the whole subject and under most of the visits. The generator runs. The door stays shut.
Stated hours, stated truth, one shut door. The machine is the easy part of the job and she knows it.
The old lines are mostly true and he is mostly willing to say which parts have stopped. Walk at dawn if you want the honest version; the rest of the day is for the settlement's confidence.

You walked the new lines with him and neither of you said the word admit. The dawn map is three routes longer than the old one and the meat came back heavier this season, which is its own kind of speech.

He teaches the migration routes that are true and retires the ones that are not, out loud, in front of the young hunters. The recovery yard eats regularly through a winter the old map would not have fed.

You asked him for the old lines as truth and he delivered them as truth. The yard went hungry twice in the hungry weeks and the settlement found out which map he was still quoting. He walks at dawn alone now, correcting it in silence.
The old lines are mostly true. Walk at dawn if you want the rest of the sentence.

The circuit is marked, posted, and paid for — by her, once, in the way that taught her. She sells meat by the schedule and terrain by the truth, and the fog month is a closed subject she closed herself.

Your tag paint is on her lines and your people walk the marked paths now. She has started paying the standing fee for the maimed into a fund instead of a pocket, which is the circuit learning from her and her from it.

The drowned fringe has a guide with posted lines and a schedule, and expeditions that use her paths come back whole. Your shelter's routes through the fringe are walked first by her, and the fee is standing and paid.

You pressed the fog question and got the whole truth, unprompted, in one piece, at a price. The circuit is marked and the meat still comes, but the paths your people walk are the ones she marked for strangers.
Marked paths, posted lines, a standing fee for the maimed, and one closed month.
The copy lessons are exact and the forged page sits face-up on the desk through all of them. She dares somebody to ask, politely, every session, and teaches the doubt whether or not anybody does.

Your people sit the lessons and learn to doubt copies properly, which is the discipline and the point. She has started leaving the desk open after class, which is as close as the archive comes to confession.

The archive's copy discipline spread to two settlements with her doubt taught in it, and the disputed page finally got its note in the margin, in her hand, dated, signed — the Marek Voln school of honesty, as the archivists now call it. Your shelter's record keeping follows her standard.
You named the page in session and the archive had to rule. The ruling acknowledged the alteration and forgave the forger and distrusted the teacher, which she predicted in writing before the vote.
Exact copy lessons and a forged page left face-up on the desk. Ask her or do not ask her. The lesson is the same.
He maps what grown-ups can stand up in, and has decided your column watches. The corridor routes he offers have never once been written down and never once been wrong.
You vouched him wages and the watching became regular. The flooded leg stays off-limits and he has started teaching two of your people the dry corridors, at exactly the speed of trust.

Your column's maps have a second layer now, drawn from memory and checked on foot: the corridors grown-ups cannot stand up in. He is apprenticed to your scout roster, on his terms, boots that fit twice included.

You told him to stop and he mostly did, for a season, until the corridor under the grid decided the matter for both of you. The leg healed crooked. The map is still in his head and slower to cross now, like him.
Corridor routes, messages run untouched, the grid as it actually is. The map stays in his head because paper can be taken off a person.
